turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Alfie and Mum, come on through. I've done his observations already, so I'll hand those over before I get back to the desk.

[SEG0002] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Lovely, thank you. We've been sat outside for ages, and the parking by the surgery is a joke, I nearly gave up and went home. He perked up a bit with a biscuit in the waiting room, which always makes me wonder if I've wasted your time.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm Dr Shah. Grab a seat. What's brought him in today?

[SEG0004] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's this fever and the cough. It started, um, I had it in my head as Monday, then I thought actually the weekend, and he's been hot and clingy and off his food. The cough is the bit that frightens me, especially at night.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): For the notes, Mum told me outside it's been two days, the home temperature was thirty-eight, and she's giving Calpol five mils four times a day.

[SEG0006] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Two days? I didn't say two days. It's been since Saturday, so five days, five-ish, I lose count of the mornings. And I never said thirty-eight, my mother's old Fahrenheit thermometer said a hundred and two point five.

[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me say it back. Fever and cough, a home reading of a hundred and two point five Fahrenheit, and the length is disputed, two days in the nurse's note and about five from you, so somewhere between two and five days. We'll sort the Calpol next.

[SEG0008] person_1 (NURSE): Obs just now: temperature thirty-eight point four, pulse a hundred and twenty-eight, breathing rate twenty-eight, oxygen ninety-six percent on air, weight eighteen point six kilograms.

[SEG0009] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Eighteen point six? That isn't right. In January at the children's clinic they said twenty-one kilos, and he hasn't stopped eating biscuits. Your scale flashed sixteen point something while he was jiggling, I saw it.
[SEG0010] person_1 (NURSE): It only counts once he stands still. I watched it settle on eighteen point six. The sixteen was movement, not his weight.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll take the settled weight, eighteen point six. The January figure is a different day. Alfie, how are you feeling?
[SEG0012] person_4 (PATIENT): Hot. And cough.

[SEG0013] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): There, he does cough. He told his dad on the phone he didn't, but that was just to get the iPad, dad's on a shift so he isn't here. At night it's constant and a bit barky, and in the day it comes when he runs about.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any hard breathing, sucking in under the ribs, or blue lips?

[SEG0015] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No, none of that. I kept looking. He isn't wheezing, not the way my nephew does, and there's no rash. I checked him all over in the bath, toes included, because you always think of meningitis, don't you.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any vomiting, diarrhoea, or ear pain?

[SEG0017] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No vomiting and no diarrhoea. He said an ear felt funny yesterday and then he said it didn't, so I don't think it's the ear. He's drinking juice more than water, and he refused his pasta, but the tummy seemed all right.
[SEG0018] person_4 (PATIENT): Tummy hurts.
[SEG0019] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Oh. You didn't say that at home. Since when, love?
[SEG0020] person_4 (PATIENT): Now.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): All right, tummy hurts just now, I'll feel it shortly. Has he had asthma, or any chest trouble on his record?

[SEG0022] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No asthma. He had bronchiolitis as a baby, about eight months, in the hospital, and they did a chest x-ray. The doctor said it was borderline, on the right side, but they didn't give antibiotics, they just watched him. I've still got the letter, not on me today.

[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): A past chest x-ray that you were told was borderline, with no antibiotics. I can't see that film, so I won't treat borderline as a number or a diagnosis I can use today. Any regular medicines, and what have you actually given for this fever?

[SEG0024] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Nothing regular. For this it's Calpol, the paracetamol liquid. I started with the five mil spoon, but he spits that, so I've been using the big spoon, which is ten mils. I aim for four times a day, though I forget the middle dose when I'm at work and my mum has him.
[SEG0025] person_1 (NURSE): That isn't what reception wrote. They've got paracetamol five mils, two hundred and fifty milligrams, four times a day. No mention of ten.

[SEG0026] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Then they wrote it down wrong. I said a spoon and they put five. It's ten mils of Calpol I've been giving, by mouth, since Saturday, when he's properly hot. He won't touch tablets.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Two doses for the same Calpol, five mils against ten, so I can't put one figure in the record. How many has he had today?

[SEG0028] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Once, this morning, and I think it was the big spoon. Fairly sure, not a hundred percent, if I'm honest. I was going to give another lot and then we got in the car.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Has he had any ibuprofen, the Nurofen?

[SEG0030] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. The bottle's in the cupboard and his dad wanted me to use that instead, we had a proper row on the phone, but I didn't give it. I can never remember if you're allowed both, so I stuck with Calpol.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ibuprofen not given, we'll leave it that way for now. Any allergies, penicillin or otherwise?

[SEG0032] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I don't think so. When he was one they gave him something for an ear infection, it might have been penicillin, and he came out in a bit of a rash. Might have been the virus though. The GP wasn't sure, I wasn't sure, and we've avoided it since just in case.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll record a possible penicillin allergy, uncertain, with a rash, not confirmed. I won't use penicillin today. Any asthma or chest problems in the family?

[SEG0034] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): My sister's little boy has asthma, that's Alfie's cousin. My husband smokes, but only outside, never in the house, and I don't. Alfie is six, in year one, and he goes to my mum's after school till about six. He doesn't smoke, obviously.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right. Let me listen to his chest and have a look in his throat and ears. Alfie, top up for me?
[SEG0036] person_4 (PATIENT): Ok.

[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Chest is clear, with good air entry, no crackles and no wheeze. Throat is a bit red. Both ears look fine, and the tummy is soft, mildly tender in the middle, with no guarding. No rash on the trunk, he's warm, and he isn't distressed.

[SEG0038] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So is the chest the problem? At three in the morning the cough sounds dreadful and I talk myself into pneumonia, and then by lunch he's playing and I feel daft for coming. There's a cake sale at school I was meant to bake for, which is neither here nor there.

[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm not calling this pneumonia, and I'm not calling it asthma. Thinking aloud, this may be a viral cough with a fever, or an early chest infection I simply can't hear yet, or a viral illness that has a mild tummy ache with it. I won't pick one of those off the story alone.
[SEG0040] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Last time they said borderline and nobody explained it. Do you want a blood test, or another chest x-ray, so someone actually looks this time?

[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): No x-ray today. If he isn't improving in three days, or if the breathing gets harder, a chest x-ray is something we might consider, not something I'm booking now. I do want a throat swab today, because the throat is red, to look for a bacterial throat infection.
[SEG0042] person_1 (NURSE): I can take that now and send it off.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): Please do. I want it sent, not left as a maybe.
[SEG0044] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He hates swabs. He screamed the place down at the flu spray last autumn, and the waiting room still remembers us, I'm sure.
[SEG0045] person_4 (PATIENT): No swab.

[SEG0046] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He says no, but we'll get it done. He's also been shattered, falling asleep on the sofa, which he never does, and shivery last night, so I put another blanket on. And he's barely eaten since yesterday lunch, apart from that biscuit and a bit of toast this morning.

[SEG0047] person_3 (DOCTOR): The tiredness and the shivers go with the fever, and eating less for a few days is common enough. For the fever I'm going to set the dose properly. Calpol Six Plus, five mils, which is two hundred and fifty milligrams, by mouth, up to four times a day, for the next three days. Not the ten mil spoon.
[SEG0048] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Five mils, even though he's got used to the big one? He's six, if that matters, and if the weight's wrong the dose might be wrong.
[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): Five mils is the usual Six Plus dose at his age, four times a day at most, for the fever. Please stop the big spoon. Don't start ibuprofen unless we've spoken again.
[SEG0050] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): All right. What about school? He's got a reading book due back, and I hate the absence text they send you.

[SEG0051] person_3 (DOCTOR): Keep him off until he's been fever-free for twenty-four hours and he's drinking. Little and often with the fluids. Come back sooner if he's working to breathe, if he stops drinking, if a rash comes up that doesn't fade, or if you're just worried.
[SEG0052] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And if it's dragging on, I book back, yes? I don't want to sit on it for a fortnight like last winter.
[SEG0053] person_3 (DOCTOR): If it's not better in three days, book back in with me. If it settles, you don't need a routine visit. We'll only ring about the swab if the result changes what he needs.
[SEG0054] person_1 (NURSE): Swab's done. He was braver than advertised. I'll send it to the lab now.
[SEG0055] person_4 (PATIENT): Done.

[SEG0056] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Thank you. I nearly forgot, his wee looked a bit dark this morning, just the once, and the next one was normal. Probably the blackcurrant juice. He hasn't been wetting the bed.
[SEG0057] person_3 (DOCTOR): One dark wee, then normal, and he's drinking juice. I'm not going after a urine infection on that, and I don't want a sample today.
[SEG0058] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And you're happy with eighteen point six for the dose? If he's really twenty-one, I've been under-dosing or over-dosing, I can't even work out which.

[SEG0059] person_3 (DOCTOR): A kilo or two doesn't move him out of that five mil, two hundred and fifty milligram dose. What stays unresolved is the five versus ten mils you've already given. I still have two stories and no single dose for that.
[SEG0060] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Fine. Little spoon from now, and dad can argue with you rather than me. I'll write it on the bottle so my mum doesn't use the big one either.
[SEG0061] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good. The swab is with the nurse. Ring us before the three days are up if he worries you, otherwise I'll see him only if it's not better.

spec.situation: Parent brings a toddler or school-age child with fever and cough; the two parents (or parent and grandparent) disagree about how long, how high, and what was given (paracetamol vs ibuprofen, doses by 'spoon'). Child says only a few words.
features: disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.
test_result_recalled: the patient reports an old test or result ('they said it was borderline'); recorded as reported history/investigation only as far as said, not as a confirmed value.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.

doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.

bad.reason: Advice supported, but responsible person is not the patient; doctor instructs family member.
